transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Aurelia CTO), Jon Rivera (Head of ML), Priya Singh (DevOps), Elliot (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): demo focused on migration/parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic to Redwood API; discussed streaming, function/ tool calling, pricing/latency tradeoffs, and security/compliance.

Topics: parity mapping, streaming vs chunking, temperature and sampling mapping, function calling and structured outputs, KV cache and batching, VPC/private deploy, SOC2/KMS, pilot next steps.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Liam, our SE, we'll run through a migration-focused demo, mapping the OpenAI/Anthropic calls to Redwood and show parity and perf notes.
[00:18] Sara (Aurelia): Thanks, excited — we want something drop-in for our clinical note summarization pipeline. Minimizing code changes and keeping latency low is critical.
[00:27] Liam (Redwood): Totally, high-level we'll show same endpoints for text/generation, streaming, function calling and embeddings, and then show a parity table — for example how "temperature" maps, top_p mapping, stop token behavior, and streaming chunking differences.
[00:43] Jon (Aurelia): Quick Q — we currently use both OpenAI and Anthropic for A/Bing certain prompts. How straightforward is the mapping, especially for Anthropic's constitutional style or the safety wrappers?
[00:54] Liam: Good question. For Anthropic prompts we've seen teams map to Redwood models with prompt templates + our safety layers; we support model variants tuned for safety. There'll be small prompt tweaks but our parity doc lists exact prompt transforms.
[01:12] Maya: I'll send that parity mapping doc after, with examples for OpenAI -> Redwood and Anthropic -> Redwood.
[01:20] Priya (Aurelia): From infra, we need to know network flows. We're likely to pilot in your hosted environment first but we'll want VPC/private later. How do VPC/private deployments look?
[01:33] Liam: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem options. For hosted we can do private networking and peering; for Private deployments you get a control plane you manage and a dedicated inference plane. We'll include a network diagram in the security pack.
[01:50] Elliot (Aurelia): Can you show streaming parity? That's a big one for our UI.
[01:56] Liam: Sure. We'll demo a streaming chat call first, here's an example where we call Redwood's /v1/generate endpoint with stream:true — you'll get token deltas similar to OpenAI's chunked responses. Note: we call them 'streams' but under the hood we preserve prefix caching and KV cache to keep latency low.
[02:18] [Screen share noise / demo starts]
[02:25] Liam: (typing) Sending a short prompt, temp 0.2, top_p 0.95, stop token '

' — you can see tokens come in incrementally.
[02:35] Sara: That looks similar. I noticed slightly bigger first-byte latency though. Is that expected?
[02:40] Liam: First-byte can vary based on model size and route; in hosted mode our default routing picks lower-latency variants for small prompt lengths. For long context loads the KV cache reduces subsequent token latency. We can tune routing to favor lower p99 latency if you need it.
[03:05] Jon: Related, how do you handle function calling / structured outputs? We rely heavily on JSON response schema enforcement.
[03:14] Liam: We support function/tool calling similar to OpenAI: you define functions and schemas, and Redwood will return structured JSON. We also have optional schema validation and automatic retries on mild schema errors. For Anthropic->Redwood mapping sometimes field names shift so the parity doc includes canonical schema examples.
[03:38] [Minor crosstalk]
[03:45] Priya: Encryption and KMS — do you support customer-managed keys when running in Private?
[03:50] Maya: Yes, KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key options for certain enterprise plans; we'll include specifics in the security pack.
[04:05] Sara: SOC 2? Audit logs? We need detailed audit trails and RBAC for clinicians.
[04:12] Maya: We're SOC 2 Type II, support SSO via SAML, granular RBAC, and audit logs per request. We'll attach the SOC 2 report and integration notes.
[04:25] Jon: On cost — how should we think about token pricing vs Anthropic? We run a lot of long-context summarizations and embeddings.
[04:34] Liam: Pricing is usage-based; for cost-sensitive workloads our Optimize tool recommends batching, KV prefix caching and quantized model variants which can reduce per-token cost. We can run a quick estimation from sample logs in the pilot.
[04:49] Sara: Pilot idea: run 10k summarizations across 3 models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Redwood) and compare latency/cost/quality. Is that feasible?
[04:58] Liam: Absolutely, that's what we usually do. We'll provide a benchmark script and can run it in your account or ours; initial smoke test would be 1k requests to catch major diffs.
[05:10] [Demo continues — showing API curl examples]
[05:18] Liam: Here's a sample curl for completions: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"model":"redwood-1.3", "prompt":"Summarize...", "temperature":0.0, "stream":true}' — behavior should match your existing OpenAI calls with minimal change.
[05:40] Sara: For embeddings, are there vector size differences vs OpenAI's ada?
[05:45] Liam: Redwood embeddings map to open standard sizes; we include comparison matrices. Often quality is similar and you can keep the same ingestion pipeline. We'll share the embeddings parity sheet.
[05:58] Jon: Are there any API incompatibilities we should watch for — e.g., stop-token edge cases or streaming chunk boundaries?
[06:06] Liam: A few gotchas: stop-token precedence when multiple stops are used, and streaming chunking when you have mid-token flush — we've documented recommended settings; generally a single stop string behaves the same. We'll call out those edge cases in the parity doc.
[06:26] [Noise — someone drops audio briefly]
[06:40] Elliot: On rollout, how can we do controlled deploys? Canary? A/B?
[06:45] Maya: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts and A/B testing per route/model and automatic fallback to a lower-cost variant if latency or errors spike. We'll include a sample rollout policy.
[06:58] Priya: For Private deployment, what's the SLA and how do we get dedicated capacity?
[07:06] Liam: Dedicated capacity is via Redwood Dedicated — reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput and SLAs. For enterprise we can negotiate commit levels; we'll include the Dedicated SLO doc.
[07:20] Sara: Anything else on compliance for healthcare (HIPAA)?
[07:24] Maya: We have customers in regulated verticals; we support data residency, private deployments and can sign a BAA. We'll coordinate legal and compliance next.
[07:36] [Demo — showing Console Optimize recommendations]
[07:40] Liam: This is Redwood Optimize — it will analyze your workload and recommend batch sizes, quantization profiles and which model variant to use for throughput vs quality tradeoffs. You can simulate cost savings before applying.
[07:57] Jon: Can Optimize recommend mapping for Anthropic style prompts?
[08:02] Liam: Yes, we have prompt transform suggestions and can score quality changes; for constitutional prompts there can be small prompt engineering tweaks.
[08:15] Sara: Are there any breaking differences between Together models and Redwood?
[08:19] Liam: Together usually differs in sampling defaults and safety behavior; parity mapping includes recommended arg changes. Most customers see 90%+ parity with a few prompt tweaks.
[08:34] [15m later — moving to Q&A and logistics]
[23:50] Maya: Recap — we'll send: 1) parity mapping doc, 2) pricing/benchmarks worksheet, 3) SOC2/security pack and KMS notes, 4) network diagram for VPC peering. Pilot kickoff week of 4/6, smoke test first then larger 10k run.
[24:06] Sara: Good. For the pilot access model, is it easier if we run in our account or in Redwood's test tenant?
[24:13] Liam: Both work. If you want accurate network latencies, run in your cloud account with a short-term dedicated capacity. If you want quick comparisons, we can run in our env with same inputs. We'll outline pros/cons in the next email.
[24:30] Priya: Firewall rules — we'll need exact egress IPs.
[24:33] Maya: We'll include IP ranges and peering details in the infra doc.
[24:40] Jon: Can you also include example migration code in our repo? A single Python adaptor would help.
[24:47] Maya: Yes, we'll attach sample SDK snippets and a small migration adapter repo.
[24:55] Elliot: Any red flags we should know right away?
[24:58] Liam: No hard red flags. A couple expected engineering tasks: small prompt tweaks for Anthropic parity and setting up KV cache/batching to hit cost targets. Both are standard and we've helped other customers through it.
[25:12] [Wrap-up]
[25:20] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and scheduling.
[25:25] Sara: Thanks, talk soon.
